body: As demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and digital services grows, opposition to new data center development is growing with it. In many communities, critics are trying to define these projects before the broader public has a chance to weigh the full picture. That’s a mistake.
For small businesses,
data centers are
not a distant tech matter. They are
part of critical infrastructure driving the platforms and services that shape how small businesses compete, grow, and innovate

in the digital economy. SBE Council’s research shows that among the 82% of small business employers using AI, for example, 93% expect to keep investing in it over the next year, 81% say AI tools are vital to their competitiveness
, and 82% believe winning the global AI race is essential to the future of the U.S. economy.

The same research shows the vast percentage of small businesses are using a wide array of digital platforms and tools. The fact that most small businesses have embedded AI and digital tools into their day-to-day operations makes the need for data centers more than a debate about land use or utility demand. It is about whether the United States will support the infrastructure that small businesses and entrepreneurs increasingly depend on to compete and grow their firms.

A fact-based discussion should absolutely take concerns seriously. But it should also flesh out the broad claims pushed by national politicians, opportunistic political candidates, and local activists where fear-based tactics are being deployed. Three of the most common myths deserve more balanced discussion.
Myth 1: Data centers do not create enough jobs or economic activity to justify the investment.
Facts: This argument usually focuses only on the permanent staffing levels inside a completed facility. That leaves out a large share of the economic activity data centers generate.

A 2025 PwC report commissioned by the Data Center Coalition found that each direct data center job supports more than six jobs elsewhere in the U.S. economy, while the industry’s total annual employment contribution reached 4.7 million jobs

in 2023. A report from the Virginia legislature’s policy analysis arm, JLARC, also found that construction is a major source of employment impact, with a single building often supporting about 1,500 workers on site at peak activity. That matters because the opportunity extends well beyond the walls of the facility itself. Data center development supports contractors and a range of other local service providers – small businesses – that help bring projects online and keep them running. For communities trying to broaden their economic base, that is meaningful activity. It is fair to ask whether a project is well-structured and well-sited. It is not fair to suggest the benefits stop with a handful of technicians.
Myth 2: Data centers are an unnecessary burden on the gri
d.
Facts: Data centers do use significant electricity and communities are right to expect serious grid planning. But opponents often present power demand as though it is the end of the story.
In reality, rising data center load is one reason utilities and policymakers are accelerating conversations about grid modernization and long-term capacity planning.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported in March 2026 that data centers are a key driver of electricity demand growth, while PwC has noted that large customers are increasingly tied to broader infrastructure planning and new approaches to managing load. The more useful question is not whether data centers consume electricity. Of course they do. The question is whether policymakers are shaping development in ways that strengthen and modernize the system to support broader economic growth. If communities want better outcomes, the answer is smart planning and accountability, not the false claim that digital infrastructure offers no value beyond its power bill.
Moreover, tech companies are exploring and pursuing a myriad of options to bring their own power (BYOP)
. Policies and elected officials need to support reasonable initiatives to enable such investment and innovative solutions.
Myth 3: Data centers are a poor use of land because they are just big buildings with little broader community value.

Facts: This criticism tends to focus on appearance rather than function. Data centers may not look like the type of development some activists prefer, but that does not make them low-value assets. They are part of the physical backbone of the digital economy. Virginia’s JLARC found that data centers can generate substantial state and local tax revenue through real estate and business personal property taxes. The Northern Virginia Technology Council similarly reported that Virginia data centers drive billions in statewide economic impact and major annual tax contributions. That revenue matters to local communities. It can help fund public priorities and expand fiscal capacity in places that want to invest in long-term growth. None of this means every proposal belongs everywhere. Community fit still matters. But the sweeping claim that data centers are inherently a bad use of land is overly broad and inappropriate for many areas.
Conclusion

The backlash against data centers is gaining momentum in some places because opponents have been effective at reducing a complex issue to a simple political target. But the small business economy deserves a fuller, fact-based conversation. SBE Council has already made clear that fear-based policymaking is the wrong approach when it comes to AI and the infrastructure supporting these tools. That same principle applies here.

Data centers support a growing small business ecosystem, strengthen local economies, and help sustain the technologies entrepreneurs are already using to compete. The right path is not blanket opposition. It is smart siting, clear standards, and a fact-based understanding of what responsible digital infrastructure can mean for American communities, entrepreneurship, and small business growth.

Introduction
Over the last several years small businesses have been increasingly using AI to build and grow their businesses.
A
Gusto
survey show
ed
that 64% of businesses
reported at least
experiment
ing
with AI
in April 2025.
Moreover, nearly two-thirds of businesses started last year used AI in order to make it easier to open
their doors.

Small businesses are finding ways to increase productivity and revenue with this technology, and those that leaned into the technology hired faster in the next twelve months following their start with AI. This analysis follows respondents to Gusto’s 2025 Main Street Meets Machine Learning survey to show how those who adopted AI changed their workforces. Our findings show that
small businesses that adopted AI
were more likely to grow their teams in the year after AI adoption. This finding is strongest at the smallest businesses: those with fewer than 10 employees
grew their teams by an average of 10%
, and small community services businesses (e.g., health care and education) grew their teams by nearly 20%.

When we took a look at the titles of those who were hired, we found that they were hiring do-ers, people who produce more of the work that business provides to its customers, suggesting that small businesses are investing time saved by implementing AI into increasing their productivity. We identified AI uses based on survey responses in April 2025. In this survey, 1,593 businesses told us that they used AI to various degrees and had been Gusto customers for long enough to track employment changes. Additionally, 669 told us that they knew about AI but had not implemented it into their business and had long enough histories on Gusto to track employment changes. This comparison group allows us to control for knowledge about and availability of AI systems. We are not comparing businesses that use AI against those who do not understand it or have never been exposed, instead we’re measuring the choice of using AI conditional on knowing about it. See our methodology section for a full list of robustness checks that further verified these results.
Key Findings

Businesses that use AI hire 7% more than those that don’t in the first year of using the technology. In the four quarters after adopting AI, a small business’s headcount rose about 7% relative to comparable firms that were aware of AI but hadn’t adopted it.
That increase built gradually, climbing from about 4.5% to about 6.8% by the end of the fourth quarter.
Businesses with fewer than 10 employees grew their teams about 10% more than comparable businesses that didn’t use AI.

This suggests that AI can make the biggest difference in resource-tight businesses. The smallest businesses, which have just as much overhead work, can focus on their core mission and grow their teams through that.

This result is broad across industries, and not just tech or professional services. Small businesses that adopted AI hired more across industries like community services, goods-producing, and personal services with small health care and social assistance firms standing out the most.
Business that use AI hire 7% more than those that don’t in the first year of using the technology

On average, small businesses that adopted AI see about 7% higher headcounts within the first year of implementing the technology than those that know about AI and choose not to use it; and by the end of the first year headcount is 6.8% greater than those who choose not to use AI. This shows that AI wasn’t a one-time hiring boost (for example, an AI engineer at a small tech startup); instead, businesses that used AI found opportunities over quarters to add to their staff. This is consistent with AI continuing to expand productivity and business output, creating additional opportunities for small businesses to expand their teams. Among the adopters that added jobs, the new roles were mostly hands-on and customer-facing. Health-care and social-assistance shops hired therapists and other care staff; elsewhere, businesses added teachers, technicians, and cooks, plus some front-desk and admin support. We can't see why any one business hired somebody, but the pattern fits a simple story: AI absorbs routine work, freeing owners to put more people on the work that serves customers. That squares with the survey, where most owners said AI made them more productive.
The strongest growth was at businesses with fewer than 10 employees

In 2025, nearly two-thirds of small businesses that used AI said that they believed that AI would make them more competitive with larger businesses. After watching their growth a year after adopting AI, we can see why. The smallest businesses, those with fewer than 10 employees, saw the largest growth: 10% or more over comparable businesses that did not use AI. For the average business with 9 employees, this means that within a year of adopting AI small businesses have already onboarded one additional employee. The mechanism here makes sense. In businesses with only a handful of employees, the owner’s time, hours, and attention are the most important resource and they’re often spent on business overhead; things like administration, scheduling, marketing, or research. Many of these businesses are too small to have established processes and resources available to protect the owner’s time to invest in their business. Larger businesses with 10-24 employees, for which we don’t measure any headcount change as a result of AI, already have much of these processes in place. Productivity for these businesses likely show up in other places than headcount, even if employees are freed to focus more on their core jobs rather than things that AI could do for them.
AI adopters hired more across industries, not just in technology or professional services

Among the smallest businesses, those that had the most to gain from AI and made use of that additional productivity by adding to their headcount, we see strong hiring across each of our four sectors. Rather than being a technology story about a very small startup hiring additional AI engineers, we see similar growth at goods-producing (e.g., construction and manufacturing) and personal services (e.g., restaurants and salons) as we do at professional services (e.g., accountants or tech firms). Small businesses as diverse as restaurants and manufacturing that adopted AI experienced similar headcount growth compared to businesses in technology and professional services that may have the most obvious use of AI. This suggests that increases in productivity as a result of AI are available for small businesses regardless of industry. The one stand-out sector in our analysis is Community services businesses. These are primarily driven by small health care and social assistance businesses. Community services businesses with fewer than 10 employees that adopted AI experienced 19% headcount growth compared to comparable businesses that did not do so. When we looked at the type of employees hired at these businesses we saw something clear: the people hired were those that provide critical community services. This included more dental hygienists at dental practices or additional therapists at mental health clinics. Increasing productivity, through making patient documentation easier, could free up staff time for more patient care. This increases access to these services in addition to increasing revenue for these small businesses.
Conclusion
Across the businesses we followed,
the ones that adopted AI went on to add more people over the next year than the ones that didn't, and the gain was largest where resources are tightest: firms with fewer than ten employees.

It showed up whether the business was a restaurant, a manufacturer, an accounting office, or a dental practice, and it didn't take a heavy technical lift. Businesses that used AI for everyday tasks saw the same hiring gains as those that had built it deep into their operations. The benefits of AI adoption don't look reserved for tech companies or the firms that can afford to go all-in. A solopreneur using AI to draft proposals and a dental office using it to speed up paperwork are both, in this data, winning back time that goes into the work their customers came for, and often into hiring the next person to help do it.
